answer.label: Older than Napoleon Hill — credited to James Freeman Clarke
answer.sourceLine: The popular imperative wording is a newspaper compression, not Napoleon Hill’s sentence. The phrase was already loose in American print by 1894, and from October 1902 papers printed it in the first person under James Freeman Clarke’s name — “If I can not do great things. I can do small things in a great way.” — more than two decades before Hill’s Law of Success ↗, which does carry a longer variant as an unattributed boxed epigram. No Clarke book containing the line has been located either, so his authorship rests on those period credit lines rather than on a primary source.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — not Hill’s wording, and in print long before him

source.excerpt: “If I cannot do great things I can do small things in a great way,” said James Freeman Clarke. It’s well to keep in mind the dignity of what is known as little things. All deeds have a moral value. The commonplace duties, even the drudgeries, may have a halo about them when done as unto the Lord.
trail: 1894 — the phrase is already loose in American print, with no author attached: an unsigned essay, “A Great Life,” in The Mirror (Stillwater, Minn.), 23 August 1894 ↗, holds that the greatest life “was built up slowly and painfully by doing small things in a great way day by day.”

1902 — the maxim appears in fixed form with a name on it, in a syndicated authors’-sentiments filler: “If I can not do great things. I can do small things in a great way.—James Freeman Clarke” ↗. The same filler ran in other papers that autumn.

1928/1933 — Napoleon Hill’s Law of Success ↗ boxes a longer, unsigned variant — “If you cannot do great things yourself, remember that you may do small things in a great way” — and by January 1933 ↗ papers were recycling that exact sentence as filler, still nameless.
1947 — the compressed imperative everyone quotes today surfaces in a Florida “Gems of Thought” column, still unattributed ↗. Hill’s name is a much later addition.

source.rightsNote: The newspaper printings shown here — 1894, 1902, 1907 — are long in the public domain as texts, and Napoleon Hill’s Law of Success was first published in 1928. But rights follow the originating work, and no originating work for this sentence has been identified: the Clarke credit rests on newspaper filler columns rather than any located book of his, and the popular imperative wording is an anonymous later reshaping. With the origin unresolved, no public-domain claim is asserted for the line itself.

author.heading: Who was James Freeman Clarke?
author.metaLine: 1810–1888 · American Unitarian minister, theologian and author
author.bio: James Freeman Clarke was a Boston Unitarian minister, abolitionist and prolific author who founded the Church of the Disciples and moved in the Transcendentalist circle around Margaret Fuller. His books — Ten Great Religions (1871), Self-Culture (1880), Every-Day Religion (1886) — were written for ordinary readers, and his recurring theme was that ordinary duties carry moral weight, which is exactly the ground this maxim stands on. He died in 1888, when Napoleon Hill was still a small child.

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: This line is pinned on Napoleon Hill across nearly every quote site. The pin has a real hook — a version of the sentence genuinely sits in one of his books — but neither the wording nor the idea originates with him.

items.why: Hill (1883–1970) did print a version, but a longer one: The Law of Success in Sixteen Lessons ↗ sets “If you cannot do great things yourself, remember that you may do small things in a great way” in a decorative box in the Master Mind lesson, with no name attached — the way that book presents dozens of aphorisms it did not originate. The maxim was already credited to someone else in newspapers by 1902 ↗, more than two decades before Hill’s book.

Clarke is the name the period sources give, but they give a first-person resolution, not an instruction: “If I cannot do great things I can do small things in a great way,” said James Freeman Clarke ↗. The imperative “do small things in a great way” that everyone repeats is a later newspaper form, and no book of Clarke’s has been found containing the sentence at all.

misattribution.truthLine: Best supported reading: an old maxim credited to James Freeman Clarke in American papers from October 1902 ↗, reshaped into today’s imperative by anonymous filler columns by 1947 ↗ — with Napoleon Hill’s name attached because a longer variant sits unsigned inside his book.

context.heading: Why this one drifted
lead: Newspapers of the early 1900s ran short filler columns — “Sentiment of Authors,” “Gems of Thought” — that swallowed a line, dropped its credit, and reshaped its grammar to fit a column inch. That is visibly what happened here: Clarke’s first-person resolution (“I can do small things in a great way”) becomes an instruction to the reader (“do small things in a great way”), and the name falls off along the way.

Napoleon Hill’s name attached later and for a mechanical reason: The Law of Success sets aphorisms in decorative boxes between blocks of text, unsigned. A reader — or a quote-site scraper — meets the line inside Hill’s book and reasonably assumes it is Hill’s. It is a common failure mode for anthologising authors, and Hill, whose biographical claims have been heavily questioned by historians, is an unusually strong magnet for it.
detailsBody: 1894 — an unsigned essay, “A Great Life,” in The Mirror (Stillwater, Minn.) argues that the greatest life “was built up slowly and painfully by doing small things in a great way day by day.” The phrase is loose in the language; no author is named.

1902–1907 — the maxim appears in fixed form, credited to James Freeman Clarke, in a syndicated authors’-sentiments filler and then in The Central Presbyterian, which builds a whole devotional item around it.

1928–1933 — Hill’s Law of Success prints the longer “if you cannot do great things yourself” version as an unsigned epigram; by 1933 newspapers are recycling that exact wording as filler, still with no name on it.
1947 — the compressed imperative that circulates today shows up in Florida “Gems of Thought” columns, again unattributed. Only much later does Hill’s name get bolted onto it.
context.pull: The filler columns kept the sentence and threw away the name.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Napoleon Hill. Credited to James Freeman Clarke in American newspapers from October 1902, fourteen years after his death; no book of Clarke's containing the line has been located, and this imperative wording is a later anonymous newspaper reshaping of the first-person sentence the period sources give him.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Northern Wisconsin Advertiser (Wabeno, Wis.), 30 October 1902, p. 2, prints in a "Sentiment of Authors" column: "If I can not do great things. I can do small things in a great way.—James Freeman Clarke."

The Central Presbyterian (Richmond, Va.), 18 December 1907, p. 12, carries an item headed "LITTLE THINGS" opening: "'If I cannot do great things I can do small things in a great way,' said James Freeman Clarke." followed by "It's well to keep in mind the dignity of what is known as little things. All deeds have a moral value."

The Mirror (Stillwater, Minn.), 23 August 1894, p. 3, carries an unsigned essay "A Great Life" containing "The greatest life ever lived was built up slowly and painfully by doing small things in a great way day by day" — with no author credited for the phrase.

Napoleon Hill's The Law of Success in Sixteen Lessons (Ralston Publishing Co., Cleveland) prints as an unsigned boxed epigram in the Master Mind lesson: "If you cannot do great things yourself, remember that you may do small things in a great way." The scan's copyright page reads "Copyright MCMXXXVII by Napoleon Hill / Copyright Prior to Revision MCMXXVIII"; the Internet Archive catalogues the item as 1928.
The Brooksville Journal (Brooksville, Fla.), 6 March 1947, p. 2, prints in an unattributed "Gems of Thought" column: "If you cannot do great things, do small things in a great way."

The Union County Times (Lake Butler, Fla.), 7 March 1947, p. 7, is the second of only two Chronicling America matches for the compressed imperative wording "do great things do small things in a great way", both from March 1947 and both unattributed.

The Western News and the Libby Times (Libby, Mont.), 26 January 1933, p. 1, runs Hill's longer wording as an unattributed filler: "If you cannot do great thin[gs, re]member that you may do small things in a great way."
Wikiquote's Napoleon Hill page does not list "If you cannot do great things, do small things in a great way" in any section, sourced or otherwise.
Wikiquote's James Freeman Clarke page does not list "If I cannot do great things, I can do small things in a great way".

James Freeman Clarke (4 April 1810 – 8 June 1888) was an American Unitarian minister, theologian and author, whose works include Ten Great Religions (1871), Self-Culture (1880) and Every-Day Religion (1886).

Napoleon Hill (26 October 1883 – 8 November 1970) was an American self-help author who published The Law of Success in 1928 and Think and Grow Rich in 1937; historians have found his central claims, including his collaboration with Andrew Carnegie, unsupported by evidence.
A Quote Investigator site search for this saying returns no article about it — QI has not investigated this quote, so there is no QI conclusion to defer to.
